planting.note: Direct sow into warm, light, sandy soil once nights stay reliably above 60F, since Souna is a fast, short-cycle landrace bred by generations of Senegalese farmers to beat an unreliable rainy season.

directions: Souna is the classic early-maturing pearl millet landrace of the Senegalese groundnut basin and Niayes region, selected over centuries for a short growth cycle that reliably sets grain even in years when the Sahelian rains arrive late or cut off early. It thrives on poor, sandy soils with minimal fertility and tolerates the long dry spells typical of the region, producing dense, bristled seed heads on tall, cane-like stalks. The small round grain is pounded or milled into couscous-style sankhal, porridge (bouillie), or flour for bread, forming a dietary staple alongside sorghum and cowpea across rural Senegal and southern Mali. Because Souna is photoperiod-sensitive to some degree and locally adapted, seed saved from Sahel-origin stock performs most consistently; harvest seed heads once fully dry and hard, then thresh and winnow by hand.
sources: ICRISAT Genetic Resources
Institut Senegalais de Recherches Agricoles (ISRA)
IRD (Institut de Recherche pour le Developpement) pearl millet landrace studies

planting.note: Direct sow early in the warm season since Sanio is a long-cycle landrace that needs a full, sustained rainy season (or steady irrigation) to fill its grain heads.

directions: Sanio is the long-cycle counterpart to the quick Souna landrace, traditionally grown in the parts of the Senegalese and Malian Sahel with more dependable rainfall where farmers can afford the extra months needed to reach maturity in exchange for a heavier grain yield. Taller and generally more productive than Souna under good rains, Sanio forms thick, elongated seed heads on robust stalks, but is more vulnerable to failure if the rains cut off early. Grain is processed the same way as other pearl millet landraces, pounded for couscous (sankhal), porridge, and flatbreads, and the dry stalks are saved as fodder and building material. Because it is adapted to the specific day-length and rainfall pattern of its home region, growers outside the Sahel should expect variable performance and treat it as a long-season warm-climate trial crop rather than a reliable short-season grain.
sources: ICRISAT Genetic Resources
Institut Senegalais de Recherches Agricoles (ISRA)
IRD (Institut de Recherche pour le Developpement) pearl millet landrace studies

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into warm, fertile soil once nights stay reliably above 60F; Jaxatu is slower to set fruit than common eggplant and needs a long, hot season.

directions: Jaxatu (also spelled diakhatou) is the small, round to oblong orange-and-cream striped fruit of a Gilo-group Solanum aethiopicum landrace central to Senegalese home cooking, distinct from the leafier Nigerian and Togolese garden-egg types grown mainly for foliage. Its firm, bitter-edged flesh is diced fresh or dried into jaxatu bi for later use, forming the signature base of soupou kandia and other tomato-and-okra Senegalese sauces where its mild bitterness balances rich, oily stews. The compact, bushy plant sets fruit over a long warm season and benefits from steady moisture and fertile soil, since erratic watering tends to intensify bitterness and reduce yield. Harvest fruit while still firm and the skin glossy; overripe fruit turns soft and overly bitter for most traditional preparations.
sources: Slow Food International Ark of Taste
World Vegetable Center (AVRDC) Solanum aethiopicum germplasm notes
True Love Seeds

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun on a raised bed or mound with excellent drainage, mimicking the Mekong Delta orchard mounds this cultivar is traditionally grown on.

directions: Nam Roi takes its name from a farming area in Binh Minh district, Vinh Long province, in Vietnam's Mekong Delta, where it has long been one of the region's most prized commercial pomelos. The fruit is pale yellow-green with thin rind and little to no bitterness in the pith, enclosing juicy, sweet-tart segments that are nearly seedless, making it a favorite for fresh eating rather than cooking or preserving. Like other pomelo, it needs a warm, frost-free, full-sun site with rich, well-drained soil and benefits from the raised planting mounds traditionally used in flood-prone delta orchards to keep roots from sitting in waterlogged ground. Thin heavy fruit sets to avoid limb breakage, and protect young trees from any frost, since pomelo wood is damaged well above freezing.
sources: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) Vietnam fruit crop profiles
Southern Horticultural Research Institute (SOFRI), Vietnam
University of California Riverside Citrus Variety Collection

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun on a raised mound with excellent drainage; Da Xanh is traditionally grown on the alluvial orchard beds of Ben Tre province in Vietnam's Mekong Delta.

directions: Da Xanh, meaning 'green skin,' is a premium pomelo selection from Ben Tre province that keeps its rind green even at full ripeness instead of yellowing like most pomelo, a trait that has made it one of Vietnam's most valuable export fruit crops. The pith is thin and the flesh a deep pink to red, firm, juicy, and nearly seedless, with a sweeter, less acidic flavor than many other pomelo selections. Give it the same culture as other pomelo: full sun, warm frost-free conditions, fertile well-drained soil, and raised beds or mounds in areas with a high water table or seasonal flooding. Fruit can be left on the tree somewhat longer than other pomelo since the green rind makes visual ripeness harder to judge, so growers typically rely on fruit size and a hollow sound when tapped to time harvest.
sources: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) Vietnam fruit crop profiles
Southern Horticultural Research Institute (SOFRI), Vietnam
University of California Riverside Citrus Variety Collection

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in well-drained soil, or grow in a large container in marginal climates so it can be sheltered from any frost.

directions: Cat Hoa Loc takes its name from Hoa Loc village in Cai Be district, Tien Giang province, in Vietnam's Mekong Delta, and is widely regarded within Vietnam as one of its finest dessert mango selections. The fruit is small to medium, oval, with thin golden-yellow skin and a small flat seed, enclosing dense, fiberless, deeply aromatic flesh that is intensely sweet with relatively low acidity compared to many other mango cultivars. Grow it exactly as other mango: full sun, excellent drainage, and protection from any frost, with reduced irrigation as fruit approaches ripeness to concentrate sugars and fragrance. Because its traditional growing region experiences a pronounced dry season that helps trigger strong flowering, growers in consistently humid or mild-winter climates may see uneven bloom and should prioritize sites with the driest, sunniest winter microclimate available.
sources: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) Vietnam fruit crop profiles
Southern Horticultural Research Institute (SOFRI), Vietnam
University of Florida IFAS Extension -- Mango Growing in the Home Landscape

common_name: Huong Chi Longan (Hung Yen Fragrant Longan)

planting.note: Plant a grafted or air-layered tree in spring; like other longan, Huong Chi needs a period of cool, relatively dry weather below about 59F to trigger strong flowering, which happens naturally in zone 9 winters.

directions: Huong Chi is one of the named cultivars behind the famous Nhan Long Hung Yen (Hung Yen caged longan) of northern Vietnam's Red River Delta, prized for generations and historically associated with offerings to the royal court. Its fruit has notably thin, smooth skin and thick, very fragrant, sweet flesh that separates cleanly from a small seed, qualities that set it apart from larger but less aromatic commercial longan selections. Grow in full sun in deep, fertile, well-drained soil, and allow the tree a relatively dry, cool period in winter to encourage heavy spring flowering, avoiding heavy nitrogen fertilization during that window so the tree sets flower buds rather than soft new growth. Hung Yen's traditional growing region has hot, humid summers and a distinct cool season, so growers in climates without a clear winter cool-down may see lighter, less reliable bloom.
sources: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) Vietnam fruit crop profiles
University of Florida IFAS Extension -- Longan Production in Florida
TFNet (International Tropical Fruits Network) -- Longan Varieties
